content: The absence of pulmonary findings in tuberculosis (TB) is not uncommon, and disseminated TB can present as a non-specific febrile illness. Extrapulmonary TB should be considered in all HIV-positive individuals presenting with TB symptoms. Specific symptoms indicating organ involvement, such as breathlessness (suggestive of pleural effusion or pericarditis), enlarged lymph nodes in the neck or armpit (lymphadenitis), or chronic headache and altered mental status (meningitis), warrant further investigation for extrapulmonary TB. Bacterial confirmation of extrapulmonary TB is often challenging due to the low sensitivity of smear microscopy and the difficulty in obtaining samples from extrapulmonary sites. Whenever possible, specimens from extrapulmonary sites should be collected. For suspected TB meningitis, the Xpert MTB/RIF test is the preferred initial diagnostic tool for cerebrospinal fluid analysis. In cases of suspected lymphadenitis, Xpert MTB/RIF can also be used to test samples obtained via lymph node biopsy or fine-needle aspiration. Additionally, LF-LAM (lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay) may aid in diagnosis, particularly in HIV-positive individuals with low CD4 cell counts. Diagnosing extrapulmonary TB is particularly complex in peripheral health facilities with limited diagnostic infrastructure. Therefore, presumptive TB treatment should be initiated in patients with danger signs, following the latest clinical algorithms. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in TB patients living with HIV is critical to reducing mortality. Detailed recommendations for co-treatment of TB and HIV are provided in clinical guidelines. HIV-positive adults and adolescents should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). Individuals with unknown or positive tuberculin skin test (TST) status who are unlikely to have active TB should receive at least six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of their degree of immunosuppression, ART status, prior TB treatment, or pregnancy. For those with unknown or positive TST status and no active TB, 36 months of IPT is recommended, irrespective of ART use or immunosuppression level. HIV-positive children without poor weight gain, fever, or current cough are unlikely to have active TB. However, children with these symptoms or a history of contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other conditions. If TB is ruled out, they should be offered IPT regardless of age. Children over 12 months of age who are unlikely to have active TB and have no TB contact should receive six months of IPT. For children under 12 months, IPT should only be given if they have had TB contact and active TB has been excluded. All children living with HIV who have completed TB treatment should receive an additional six months of IPT. Isoniazid 300 mg daily prevents the progression of latent TB infection to active disease. The combined use of IPT and ART has shown benefits in TB prevention and mortality reduction, even in individuals with higher CD4 counts. TST is not required to initiate IPT in people with HIV, but it is encouraged where feasible, as TST-positive individuals not on ART benefit more from IPT. Healthcare workers should use particulate respirators (e.g., N95 masks) when caring for patients with infectious TB. Patients and families should be educated on cough etiquette, avoiding crowded settings, and spending time outdoors to minimize transmission. MDR-TB, resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, poses significant challenges in HIV-positive individuals due to limited treatment options and poorer outcomes. XDR-TB, which is resistant to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable drugs, has been observed to spread rapidly among people living with HIV. ART is recommended for all HIV-positive patients with drug-resistant TB, initiated as early as possible within eight weeks of starting TB treatment. Novel anti-TB drugs like delamanid and bedaquiline may be used cautiously in specific populations, though data on their safety and efficacy remain limited. Cryptococcal meningitis is a leading cause of death in HIV-positive individuals, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Delayed presentation and limited access to treatment contribute to high mortality rates. Routine antifungal prophylaxis is not recommended unless ART initiation is significantly delayed. For treatment, amphotericin B combined with flucytosine is preferred, followed by fluconazole for consolidation and maintenance therapy. ART initiation should be delayed in cryptococcal meningitis to reduce the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-infections are common in people living with HIV, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. HIV accelerates the progression of HBV-related liver disease, increasing the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. ART should be provided to all individuals co-infected with HIV and HBV, prioritizing those with severe chronic liver disease. Tenofovir (TDF) with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) is recommended for treating HIV-HBV co-infection. All newly diagnosed HIV patients should be screened for HBV and vaccinated if non-immune. HCV-related liver disease progresses more rapidly in HIV co-infected individuals. Comprehensive care, including prevention, testing, and treatment, is essential for managing HIV-HCV co-infection.
